title: Embedded Wallets: How They Work and Generate Revenue
summary: An embedded wallet is a crypto wallet built directly into an application so users can access digital assets without opening a separate wallet app, managing browser extensions, or handling a seed phrase at onboarding.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


-


An embedded wallet lets users hold, send, receive, or use digital assets inside an application without leaving the product flow.


-


For businesses, embedded wallets provide account infrastructure for payments, stablecoin transfers, trading, rewards, and premium account features.


-


Product and developer teams decide how to handle key management, transaction policy, chain support, recovery, compliance workflow, and SDK scope.


-


The core tradeoff is control. Custodial models may reduce user friction and improve recovery. Non-custodial or hybrid models shift more responsibility to the user and product design.


An embedded wallet is a crypto wallet built directly into an application so users can access digital assets without opening a separate wallet app, managing browser extensions, or handling a seed phrase at onboarding. It turns wallet creation, signing, and asset movement into part of the product experience.


Fintech platforms, consumer apps, enterprise software providers, marketplaces, and payment operators use embedded wallets to add payments and stablecoin transfers, rewards and trading, treasury flows, or asset access inside an existing user interface. In some cases, this becomes the account system for a digital asset banking product (a bank-like account experience, not a chartered or licensed banking entity), where users can hold balances, move funds, and access financial functions from one account. Users see one account. The business gains new product surface area, data, retention, and monetization paths.


Teams evaluating infrastructure can start with embedded wallet infrastructure.


## Embedded vs. Connected Wallets


For fintechs, a core product decision is between embedded vs connected wallets. An embedded wallet is created and managed inside the application experience. A connected wallet is controlled by the user outside the application, then connected through a browser extension, mobile wallet, WalletConnect flow, or similar interface.


The decision affects conversion, control, liability, integration scope, signing flow, recovery, and support burden. An embedded crypto wallet usually fits products that need low-friction onboarding, repeat transactions, account abstraction, or business-controlled policy layers. A connected wallet fits products serving users who already manage their own keys and expect direct wallet control.

## How Embedded Wallets Work


An embedded wallet starts when the application creates a wallet for a user, business, account, or internal entity through an API or SDK. The wallet may be generated at signup, after identity verification, when the user first receives assets, or when a specific feature is activated. The application then maps that wallet to the user’s account in its own ledger, database, permissions model, and support workflow.


The technical system has four main layers.


-


Wallet creation generates or assigns addresses.


-


Key management determines who can sign and recover transactions.


-


Transaction signing approves asset movement according to the selected cryptographic model.


-


Policy enforcement applies controls before a transaction can move on-chain.


At the product level, embedded wallets let the application offer crypto or stablecoin functionality without making users confront raw blockchain mechanics. At the technical level,[wallet infrastructure](https://www.bitgo.com/products/wallet-as-a-service/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=embedded_wallets_how_they_work) must connect with authentication, account state, transaction queues, webhooks, chain indexing, error handling, and compliance checks.


A well-designed embedded crypto wallet creates an address. It defines who can initiate a transfer, supported assets, limits and approvals, failure handling, and reconciliation with internal account records.


## Embedded Wallet Key Management and Security


Key management is the main design decision behind an embedded wallet. It determines who controls assets, who can recover access, who can approve movement, and where liability may sit if something fails. Teams choose the model based on the product, jurisdiction, user base, and risk tolerance.


In a custodial model, a regulated or contracted custodian controls the private keys and executes transfers after required checks. This can simplify user recovery and support. It can also create custody, compliance, and contractual obligations. In a non-custodial model, the user or business retains key control. That can reduce direct custody exposure. Recovery, device loss, and user education become harder product problems.


Custodial and non-custodial models can both use different signing technologies, including MPC.[MPC crypto wallets](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/mpc-crypto-wallets-multi-party-computation-security/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=embedded_wallets_how_they_work) distribute signing across multiple key shares, allowing a transaction to be authorized without reconstructing a private key in one place. Depending on the implementation, MPC can support approval workflows, separation of duties, and recovery processes.


Security also depends on operating controls. Teams need transaction limits, role-based approvals, address allowlists, fraud monitoring, audit logs, and incident/recovery procedures. The central question is whether the operating model stays secure when users lose devices, staff change roles, chains pause, transactions fail, or attackers target support workflows.


## How to Add an Embedded Wallet to Your App


Adding an embedded wallet starts with the operating model. The team first selects a provider and key management model. That decision defines the legal structure, recovery process, signing workflow, and what the user will experience during onboarding, transfer approval, and support escalation.


Next, the team configures wallet policies. These policies should cover transaction limits, approval roles, supported destinations, asset/geographic permissions, and exception handling. Policies also need to map to internal roles, such as product administrators, compliance reviewers, finance teams, and support operators.


The[embedded wallet SDK](https://www.bitgo.com/products/wallet-as-a-service/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=embedded_wallets_how_they_work) then connects the application to wallet and address creation, transaction initiation/signing, status monitoring, and notifications. Developer teams need to test the SDK in a sandbox and in real product flows. That includes failed signatures, delayed or duplicate requests, unsupported assets, network-fee changes, and abandoned transfers.


Configure chain support before launch. Teams need to decide which assets, networks, and transaction types are available at launch, then define how new chains will be added without forcing users to migrate wallets. Before production, test recovery, compliance review, blocked transfers, webhook failures, balance reconciliation, and support/incident response.


The output should be a wallet feature that works inside application flows and remains governed by explicit controls. This separates a governed product capability from an uncontrolled crypto add-on.


## How Embedded Wallets Generate Revenue


Embedded wallets generate revenue when the product charges for wallet-based actions or account tiers. They provide account infrastructure for revenue models that would otherwise be unavailable or harder to deliver inside the application. The wallet becomes the account layer for crypto, stablecoins, payments, rewards, transfers, and other balance-based features.


For platforms building toward a digital asset banking experience (not a chartered banking license), the wallet is often the account system behind the commercial model. It gives the platform a way to support balances, transfers, payments, conversions, and reporting without sending users to an external crypto wallet.


The most direct model is transaction revenue. A platform can charge a fee when users send assets, withdraw funds, swap assets, move stablecoins, or use payment features. For high-frequency products, small per-transaction fees can become recurring revenue. Pricing has to remain visible, consistent, and aligned with the user benefit of the action.


Conversion spread is another common model. When users move between fiat, stablecoins, and crypto assets, the platform may earn a spread or fee on the conversion. This resembles other financial application models where convenience, liquidity, and integrated execution justify a clearly disclosed cost.


Wallets also support premium account tiers. A platform can charge businesses or advanced users for higher limits, faster settlement, approval controls, reporting, and multi-entity administration/dedicated support. In enterprise settings, platforms often monetize workflow control, reliability, reporting, and operational scale.


Payment acceptance can create another revenue path. A platform that allows merchants, creators, vendors, or marketplaces to accept stablecoin payments can charge transaction fees, monthly platform fees, or value-added service fees. Where permitted and supported, balance-based products may also include rewards or yield-sharing structures, but those models require careful legal, product, and disclosure review.


Teams that want to add[crypto functionality inside their app](https://www.bitgo.com/products/crypto-as-a-service/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=embedded_wallets_how_they_work) should treat monetization as a product architecture question. The wallet defines what users can do. The business model defines which of those actions become sustainable revenue. For a broader look at how financial institutions can build digital asset products and revenue opportunities, explore BitGo’s[Crypto Infrastructure for Banks Report](https://landing.bitgo.com/rs/552-OGK-141/images/BitGo_Banks_Report.pdf?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=bitgo_for_banks&utm_campaign=embedded_wallets_revenue&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=embedded_wallets_how_they_work) .


## Compliance Considerations for Embedded Wallet Platforms


Adding an embedded wallet can change the compliance profile of an application. Obligations vary by jurisdiction, user location, asset type, custody model, and payment functions such as transfers, exchange, staking, rewards, or merchant acceptance.


The compliance review becomes more important when the product resembles a digital asset bank from the user’s perspective. Even if the platform does not describe itself that way, regulators and partners may focus on the actual functions offered, including custody, transfers, conversion, payments, and account access.


Common review areas include money transmission, identity and AML controls, sanctions and[Travel Rule workflows](https://www.bitgo.com/resource-center/travel-rule/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=embedded_wallets_how_they_work) , consumer disclosures, stablecoin-specific obligations, and record/complaint handling. A non-custodial interface can have different obligations than a custodial account product. Product details control the analysis. A platform that controls user onboarding, transfer permissions, conversion, or payment routing may still need compliance workflows around those activities.


It’s important to build compliance design into the wallet flow before launch. Identity checks, risk scoring, blocked-address controls, approval queues, audit logs/reporting, and support escalation should be part of the wallet system.

## FAQs


### What are the tradeoffs between custodial and non-custodial embedded wallets?


Custodial models can simplify recovery and support. They may create direct custody and compliance obligations. Non-custodial models can shift more key control to the user or business. They require stronger recovery, education, and support design. Teams evaluating key-control alternatives can compare[self-custody wallet options](https://www.bitgo.com/products/self-custody/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=embedded_wallets_how_they_work) .


### How does key management work if a user loses their device or credentials, and who is responsible for recovery?


Recovery follows the selected model. Custodial wallets usually rely on provider-controlled verification and recovery workflows. Non-custodial and hybrid wallets may use backup keys, social recovery, passkeys, or external signers. Responsibility should be defined in contracts, user terms, and support procedures.


### Which parts of embedded wallet integration can be offloaded to BitGo’s SDK?


The SDK can usually reduce work around wallet creation, address generation, signing, transaction monitoring, and network connectivity. Effort still goes into authentication, UX/account mapping, compliance logic, reconciliation/testing, and analytics/support tooling. Scope varies by custody model, chains, assets, and launch requirements.


### How do embedded wallets handle gas fees so users can transact without native tokens?


Platforms can handle gas through sponsored transactions, fee abstraction, stablecoin-denominated fees, internal billing, or pre-funded operational wallets. Choose the approach based on the chain, asset, user flow, and custody model. The goal is to prevent users from needing a separate native-token balance before they can transact.


### What compliance obligations do fintechs that use embedded wallets inherit the moment they let users hold or move assets inside their app?


Obligations may include KYC/AML, sanctions screening, money transmission analysis, Travel Rule workflows, stablecoin disclosures, transaction monitoring, and recordkeeping. The analysis turns on jurisdiction, custody model, asset type, user base, and whether the app supports transfers, conversion, rewards, or payments.


### How do fintechs that use embedded wallets handle chain support and upgrades without forcing users to migrate wallets?


Choose infrastructure that supports multi-chain wallet operations, configurable asset support, and a clear asset-support process. The application should separate user account identity from chain-specific addresses so new networks can be added without rebuilding the customer account model. Test migrations and unsupported-asset scenarios before launch.
